context.heading: Funding the chorus
context.body: "Add to your faith" uses epichorēgeō, from the chorēgos, a wealthy citizen who paid for a city's festival chorus and was expected to do it lavishly. Peter asks believers to supply virtue on virtue with the same generosity. He uses the same verb in verse 11: God will "richly supply" their entrance into the eternal kingdom.

context.heading: A tent and an exodus
context.body: Peter calls his body a "tent" (v. 13) and his death an exodos, "departure" (v. 15). Both words echo the transfiguration, where Moses and Elijah spoke of Jesus' exodos (Luke 9:31) and Peter offered to build tents. Facing death, he reaches back to the mountain he describes a few verses later.

context.heading: Not clever myths
context.body: Peter denies following "cleverly devised myths" (muthoi), the word for stories about the gods. Instead the apostles were epoptai, "eyewitnesses", a term sometimes used for initiates who reached the highest stage of seeing in Greek mystery cults. Peter's claim is plainer: he saw Jesus' majesty with his own eyes.

theology.title: Everything needed for godliness
theology.body: God's divine power "has given us everything we need for life and godliness" (v. 3). The list of virtues in verses 5–7 starts with faith and ends with love, but it rests on what God has already given. This is growth from grace, not self-improvement to earn it.

theology.title: The Father's voice on the mountain
theology.body: On the mountain the Father said, "This is My beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased" (v. 17), echoing Psalm 2:7 and Isaiah 42:1. The Father honors the Son, and Peter hears the Old Testament's promised King and Servant confirmed in Jesus.

theology.title: A lamp until the morning star
theology.body: Prophetic Scripture is "a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts" (v. 19). The morning star may echo Numbers 24:17, the star from Jacob. God's word guides now, and Christ Himself will one day fill the sky.

application.title: Forgetting you were forgiven
application.body: Peter says the one who lacks these qualities "has forgotten that he has been cleansed from his past sins" (v. 9). Spiritual stagnation often starts with amnesia about grace.
application.question: When did the fact that you are forgiven last change how you treated someone?

application.title: Reminders are not beneath you
application.body: Peter writes to people who "know these things" and reminds them anyway, for as long as he lives (vv. 12–13). Mature Christians still need the basics repeated.
application.question: Which basic truth of the faith do you quietly assume you have outgrown?

context.heading: Smuggled in
context.body: False teachers will "secretly introduce" (pareisagō) destructive heresies, a verb for bringing something in alongside, like contraband. Paul uses a related word for "false brothers secretly brought in" (Galatians 2:4). False teaching rarely arrives labeled; it slips in next to true things and sounds close enough to pass.

context.heading: Trading in people
context.body: In their greed, false teachers will "exploit" you (emporeuomai, to trade or do business, the root of "emporium"). Their words are plastos, "made up", a word for something molded like clay. Peter pictures teachers treating listeners as merchandise and shaping their message to fit what sells.

context.heading: Tartarus
context.body: God cast sinning angels into hell, using the verb tartaroō, found only here. In Greek myth Tartarus was the deepest pit beneath the underworld, where rebel Titans were imprisoned. Peter borrows a word his readers knew. He also seems to draw on Jewish traditions about angels who sinned before the flood (Genesis 6:1–4), though details are debated.

theology.title: He knows the difference
theology.body: God judged the ancient world but kept Noah, and destroyed Sodom but rescued Lot (vv. 5–8). Peter even calls Lot "righteous", though Genesis 19 shows his failures. God's judgment is never careless; He knows exactly whom to rescue, and His mercy reaches flawed people who still belong to Him.

theology.title: Denying the Master who bought them
theology.body: False teachers deny "the Master who bought them" (v. 1). Christians differ on how this verse relates to the scope of Christ's atoning death, whether it means they were truly redeemed or only claimed to be. All agree the charge is severe: they reject the One whose ownership they once professed.

application.title: Freedom that enslaves
application.body: False teachers promise freedom while being slaves themselves, "for people are slaves to whatever has mastered them" (v. 19). Many habits begin as liberation and end as a master.
application.question: What habit once promised you freedom but now makes your decisions for you?

application.title: Check the fruit, not the charisma
application.body: Peter's marks of false teachers are mostly about character: greed, sexual exploitation, arrogance and contempt for authority. Polished delivery tells you nothing about any of those.
application.question: Which teachers or influencers do you follow without ever checking how they handle money, sex and power?

context.heading: Scoffers and the sleeping fathers
context.body: Scoffers (empaiktai, mockers) say, "Ever since our fathers fell asleep, everything goes on as it has" (v. 4). The "fathers" are probably the first generation of believers, now dying. If Jesus had not returned while the apostles lived, critics argued, perhaps He never would. Jude 18 warns of the same mockers.

context.heading: Elements dissolved
context.body: The stoicheia, "elements", will be dissolved by fire (v. 10). The word meant basic components, like the four elements of Greek thought, and could also mean heavenly bodies. Ancient manuscripts differ on whether the earth will be "burned up" or "found", that is, laid bare. Interpreters debate whether Peter means annihilation or purifying renewal.

context.heading: Hastening the day
context.body: Believers wait for and "hasten" (speudō) the day of God (v. 12). The verb can mean to hurry something along or to desire it eagerly. Some later Jewish teachers held that Israel's repentance could hasten the Messiah. Peter may mean something similar: holy living, prayer and witness are not idle waiting.

theology.title: The word that made, flooded and will renew
theology.body: By God's word the heavens and earth came to be, by water the world was flooded, and by the same word the present world is kept for judgment (vv. 5–7; Genesis 1; 6–9). History is not a closed loop that "goes on as it has". God has acted decisively before, and He will again.

theology.title: Glory to Jesus forever
theology.body: The letter ends, "To Him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity" (v. 18). Doxologies like this were given to God, and Peter gives it to Jesus Christ. It is a quiet confession that Jesus shares the Father's divine glory.

application.title: Delay is not indifference
application.body: God is not slow in keeping His promise but patient (v. 9). What feels like absence may be mercy still at work.
application.question: What delay in your life are you reading as God's indifference rather than His patience?

application.title: Possessions with an expiry date
application.body: If everything here will be laid bare, Peter asks, "what kind of people ought you to be?" (v. 11). The things we protect most anxiously are usually the ones that will not last.
application.question: Which possession or status would you worry about less if you really believed it will not survive the day of the Lord?

application.title: Bending hard verses
application.body: Some people twist hard parts of Scripture "to their own destruction" (v. 16). It is easy to read a difficult passage until it agrees with what we already wanted.
application.question: Which passage have you bent to fit what you already wanted it to say?
